card.name: Sakela Sili
card.profile: Sakela Sili is the ritual circle dance of the Kirat Rai (Khambu) of eastern Nepal, performed during the biannual Sakela/Sakewa festivals — Ubhauli (spring) and Udhauli (autumn). "Sili" means steps; dancers move in a circle led by a Silimangpa and Silimangma, mimicking birds and animals and depicting agricultural cycles to Sili kane drums and cymbals. Rooted in the oral Mundhum scripture and nature worship; revitalized as ethnic-identity practice from 1981. Indigenous form — ethnographic record.
card.insight: Ethnographer Martin Wettstein notes a diaspora YouTube-driven "rising trend" of Sakela, with "dance" only a loose translation of an embodied way of moving. (Routledge, 2019)

card.profile_long: Sakela Sili is the defining ritual dance of the Kirat Rai (Khambu) people, an indigenous ethnic group primarily residing in eastern Nepal, as well as the Sikkim, Kalimpong, and Darjeeling regions of India. The dance is inextricably linked to the Sakela festival, which is celebrated twice annually: Ubhauli, marking the start of the farming year in the month of Baisakh (April–May), and Udhauli, held during the harvest season in the month of Mangsir (November–December). These festivals are rooted in the shamanistic and animistic beliefs of the Kirat people, serving as a formal prayer to Mother Nature for healthy crops and protection from natural calamities. The dance is performed in large, inclusive circles where people of all ages participate, reinforcing social cohesion and cultural identity. The core of the performance is the 'sili,' a series of choreographed movements that represent the relationship between human life and the natural world. Each circle is guided by a male leader, the Silimangpa, and a female leader, the Silimangma. These leaders dictate the choreography, which the rest of the group follows in unison. The dance is not merely a performance but a ritualistic act of devotion to Bhumi Dev, the Earth goddess. The nomenclature for the dance varies significantly across the different Kirat sub-tribes and languages; for instance, while the Chamling call it Sakela, the Bantawa use the terms Sakewa or Sakenwa, and the Thulung refer to it as Toshi. Despite these linguistic variations, the practice is recognized as a shared cultural pillar among the Kirat. The dance is performed in traditional attire, which adds a visual layer of cultural significance to the rhythmic movements. The ritual is a living tradition, maintained by the community to preserve their connection to the land and their ancestral heritage. While the Yakkha and Limbu people have their own distinct traditions, such as Youchyang and Chasok Tangnam, the Sakela Sili remains a central expression of Kirat identity, bridging the gap between the agricultural calendar and the spiritual life of the community.

card.sacred_note: The dance is a ritual prayer to Mother Nature and the Earth goddess Bhumi Dev; it is performed with spiritual intent as part of the Kirat Mundhum tradition.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originates from the shamanistic and animistic traditions of the Kirat people, documented as a prayer to Mother Nature for agricultural prosperity. It is tied to the Kirat Mundhum, the oral scripture of the community.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Participants form a large circle, with all ages dancing together. The movement is led by a Silimangpa (male) and a Silimangma (female), who choreograph the 'sili' steps while the group follows. The movements are intended to reflect aspects of human life and nature.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is accompanied by drums and cymbals, which provide the rhythmic foundation for the ritual performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear traditional Kirat attire. The dance takes place in large, open spaces suitable for communal circle formations, often during the festivals of Ubhauli and Udhauli.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Celebrated on Baisakh Purnima for Ubhauli and on the full moon of Mangsir for Udhauli, the dance acts as a prayer for crop health and a thanksgiving for the harvest.
sections.notable_figures: The Silimangpa (male leader) and Silimangma (female leader) are the central figures responsible for leading the circle and choreographing the sili.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is known by various names including Sakewa, Sakenwa, Toshi, Segro, Iksamang, Balipuja, and Fagulak, depending on the specific Rai language group.
sections.lineage: The dance is part of the broader Kirat cultural tradition, sharing roots with other Kirat practices while maintaining its distinct identity within the Khambu community.

claims.text: Sakela is a festival of the Khambu (Rai people) in eastern Nepal and parts of India.
The festival is celebrated twice a year as Ubhauli and Udhauli.
The dance is a prayer to Mother Nature for healthy crops and protection.
The dance is performed in a large circle led by male and female leaders.
The term 'sili' refers to movements reflecting the relationship between humans and nature.
The dance is a living tradition among the Kirat people.
